title: Ein deutsches Requiem (A German Requiem)
hook: Not a Mass for the dead but comfort for the living, in words Brahms chose himself from Luther’s Bible.

painting.title: The Jewish Cemetery
painting.pairingNote: Tombs, a ruined church and a dead tree under a breaking storm, with a rainbow over them; like the Requiem, Ruisdael sets the passing of all things beside a promise of hope.

facts: A requiem is usually the Catholic Mass for the dead, sung in Latin, praying for the souls of the departed. Brahms, a Protestant from Hamburg, did something different. He chose his own texts from Martin Luther’s German Bible, and his first words are for those left behind: “Blessed are they that mourn, for they shall be comforted.” He said he would gladly have called it “a human Requiem”. “German” refers to the language.

His mother died in February 1865, and the loss probably moved him to write it; the death of his mentor Robert Schumann in 1856 may also lie behind it. The second movement uses music he had sketched in 1854, the year of Schumann’s breakdown. By August 1866 six movements were finished.

The first three movements were tried out in Vienna on 1 December 1867, and the performance went badly. The first full performance of the six movements, in Bremen Cathedral on Good Friday, 10 April 1868, with Brahms conducting, was a great success and made his name.

In May 1868 he added a movement for soprano, now the fifth, with the words “I will comfort you, as one whom his mother comforteth”. The complete work in seven movements was first heard in Leipzig on 18 February 1869. It is Brahms’s longest work.
bigPicture.inOneLine: comfort for the mourners (I), all flesh is as grass (II), a man asks how long his life will be (III), the lovely dwellings of the Lord (IV), a mother’s comfort (V), the last trumpet and death’s defeat (VI), and blessed are the dead (VII).

movements.heading: Selig sind, die da Leid tragen
movements.title: Selig sind, die da Leid tragen
movements.summary: “Blessed are they that mourn.” A soft, dark opening without violins: only the lower strings, horns and woodwinds, over a long held bass note. The choir enters almost in a whisper. In the middle the music moves from tears to joy: those who sow in tears shall reap in joy.

mainIdeas.name: The colour
mainIdeas.description: no violins at all in this movement, so the sound stays low and warm, with divided violas and cellos.

mainIdeas.name: The choir’s first phrase
mainIdeas.description: a gentle rising step, then a softer fall, on “Selig sind”.

stops.hear: A low, held note; violas and cellos weave a slow, dark melody above it
stops.happening: The orchestral introduction, without violins

stops.hear: The choir enters very softly, unaccompanied for a moment
stops.happening: “Selig sind, die da Leid tragen” (“Blessed are they that mourn”, Matthew 5:4)

stops.hear: A warmer phrase, rising
stops.happening: “denn sie sollen getröstet werden” (“for they shall be comforted”)

stops.hear: The key shifts to a softer, darker colour
stops.happening: “Die mit Tränen säen” (“They that sow in tears”, Psalm 126:5)

stops.hear: The music walks on with a heavier tread, then lifts and grows louder
stops.happening: “Sie gehen hin und weinen … und kommen mit Freuden” (“They go forth and weep … and come again with joy”)

stops.hear: The opening words and music return
stops.happening: “Selig sind” again

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: The harp joins for the first time, rippling softly as the music fades
stops.happening: The close, on “getröstet” (“comforted”)

notice: Listen for the moment the harp appears at the very end. It is the first time you hear it, and it brings a sudden light.

movements.heading: Denn alles Fleisch, es ist wie Gras
movements.title: Denn alles Fleisch, es ist wie Gras
movements.summary: A funeral march, but in three beats instead of two, slow and heavy, with timpani pounding beneath. “For all flesh is as grass, and all the glory of man as the flower of grass.” A lighter section asks for patience, like the farmer waiting for rain. The march returns, louder, and then the music bursts into the major: “But the word of the Lord endureth for ever”, and a joyful, fast section about the redeemed coming home.

mainIdeas.name: The march
mainIdeas.description: a slow tread in three, muted strings, the choir singing the melody quietly in [[unison|unison]] at first.

mainIdeas.name: The answer
mainIdeas.description: a fast, bright B-flat major, the voices entering one after another.

stops.hear: Muted strings and soft timpani beat out a slow march in three
stops.happening: The introduction

stops.hear: The choir enters quietly, all singing the same tune
stops.happening: “Denn alles Fleisch, es ist wie Gras” (“For all flesh is as grass”, 1 Peter 1:24)

stops.hear: The march returns at full force: loud choir, brass and pounding timpani
stops.happening: The same words, now overwhelming

stops.hear: Lighter and more flowing, in a warmer key
stops.happening: “So seid nun geduldig” (“Be patient therefore”, James 5:7)

stops.hear: The march once more, quiet, then crushing
stops.happening: “Denn alles Fleisch” again

stops.hear: A sudden turn to the major; the choir declares loudly
stops.happening: “Aber des Herrn Wort bleibet in Ewigkeit” (“But the word of the Lord endureth for ever”, 1 Peter 1:25)

stops.hear: Fast and joyful: the voices enter one after another and the music races
stops.happening: “Die Erlöseten des Herrn werden wiederkommen” (“The ransomed of the Lord shall return”, Isaiah 35:10)

stops.hear: A great climax on “ewige Freude” (“everlasting joy”)
stops.happening: Joy and gladness overcome sorrow

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: The music settles and fades quietly
stops.happening: “Schmerz und Seufzen wird weg müssen” (“Sorrow and sighing shall flee away”)

notice: The march is in three beats, not the usual two. Try counting it: the slow, dragging step makes it feel heavier than a normal march.

movements.heading: Herr, lehre doch mich
movements.title: Herr, lehre doch mich
movements.summary: The baritone soloist sings a prayer: “Lord, teach me that I must have an end.” The choir takes up his words. Doubt grows, “my life is as nothing before thee”, until the question “Lord, what do I wait for?” turns to “my hope is in thee”. The movement ends with a [[fugue|fugue]] over a single low D held for the whole section.

mainIdeas.name: The prayer
mainIdeas.description: the baritone alone, answered by the choir with the same words.

mainIdeas.name: The fugue
mainIdeas.description: a strong subject passed between the voices, all resting on a held bass note.

stops.hear: A short, quiet introduction, then the baritone alone
stops.happening: “Herr, lehre doch mich” (“Lord, make me to know mine end”, Psalm 39:4)

stops.hear: The choir repeats the baritone’s words
stops.happening: The personal prayer becomes everyone’s

stops.hear: The music grows restless and anxious
stops.happening: “Ach, wie gar nichts sind alle Menschen” (“Surely every man is altogether vanity”, Psalm 39:5–6)

stops.hear: A pause, a question, then the music turns to D major
stops.happening: “Nun, Herr, wes soll ich mich trösten? Ich hoffe auf dich” (“And now, Lord, what wait I for? My hope is in thee”, Psalm 39:7)

stops.hear: A strong, confident fugue, with one low note held underneath the whole time
stops.happening: “Der Gerechten Seelen sind in Gottes Hand” (“The souls of the righteous are in the hand of God”, Wisdom 3:1). The held note is a [[pedal-note|pedal note]]

stops.label: Last 20 seconds
stops.hear: A final, ringing chord in D major
stops.happening: The end of the fugue

notice: In the fugue, listen to the very bottom of the orchestra: the same low D sounds without a break from the beginning of the fugue to its end.

movements.heading: Wie lieblich sind deine Wohnungen
movements.title: Wie lieblich sind deine Wohnungen
movements.summary: The centre of the work, and its calmest movement: a gentle waltz-like song in three beats, “How lovely are thy dwellings, O Lord of hosts”. It is often sung on its own.

mainIdeas.name: The melody
mainIdeas.description: a falling, swaying phrase in the woodwinds, then in the choir.
A livelier middle section in which the voices overlap.

stops.hear: Woodwinds play a gentle, swaying tune; the choir answers softly
stops.happening: “Wie lieblich sind deine Wohnungen” (“How lovely are thy dwellings”, Psalm 84:1)

stops.hear: A warmer, more longing phrase
stops.happening: “Meine Seele verlanget” (“My soul longeth”)

stops.hear: Livelier: the voices enter one after another
stops.happening: “Die loben dich immerdar” (“They will be still praising thee”, Psalm 84:4)

stops.label: Near the end
stops.hear: The opening phrase returns and fades
stops.happening: A peaceful close

notice: Notice the lilt of three beats to a bar. After two dark movements, it is the first music that almost dances.

movements.heading: Ihr habt nun Traurigkeit
movements.title: Ihr habt nun Traurigkeit
movements.summary: The movement Brahms added after the Bremen premiere. The soprano soloist sings “You now have sorrow, but I will see you again.” Under her the choir sings, slowly and softly, “I will comfort you, as one whom his mother comforteth”. Many hear in it Brahms’s grief for his own mother, though he never said so.

mainIdeas.name: The choir’s line
mainIdeas.description: slow, even notes underneath, like a steady hand.

stops.hear: Soft strings, then the soprano alone, high and gentle
stops.happening: “Ihr habt nun Traurigkeit” (“Ye now therefore have sorrow”, John 16:22)

stops.hear: The choir enters below her in slow, quiet notes
stops.happening: “Ich will euch trösten” (“I will comfort you”, Isaiah 66:13)

stops.hear: The soprano sings a new phrase in a brighter key
stops.happening: “Sehet mich an” (“Behold with your eyes”, Sirach 51:27)

stops.hear: The choir’s comforting words return, the soprano soaring above
stops.happening: “wie einen seine Mutter tröstet” (“as one whom his mother comforteth”)

stops.label: Near the end
stops.hear: Soprano and choir fade together
stops.happening: A quiet close

notice: Listen to the two layers at once: the soprano moving freely above, the choir moving slowly below.

movements.heading: Denn wir haben hie keine bleibende Statt
movements.title: Denn wir haben hie keine bleibende Statt
movements.summary: The most dramatic movement. “For here we have no lasting city.” The baritone announces a mystery: we shall all be changed, at the last trumpet. The music explodes into a fast, stormy section, “Death, where is thy sting?”, and ends with a great [[fugue|fugue]] in C major: “Lord, thou art worthy to receive glory.”

mainIdeas.name: The wandering
mainIdeas.description: soft, uncertain steps in the choir, over plucked strings.

mainIdeas.name: The storm
mainIdeas.description: fast, loud, in three beats, with the full orchestra.

mainIdeas.name: The fugue
mainIdeas.description: a long, broad subject in C major, built up voice by voice.

stops.hear: The choir sings softly, as if wandering, over [[pizzicato|pizzicato]] strings
stops.happening: “Denn wir haben hie keine bleibende Statt” (“For here have we no continuing city”, Hebrews 13:14)

stops.hear: The baritone alone, mysterious
stops.happening: “Siehe, ich sage euch ein Geheimnis” (“Behold, I shew you a mystery”, 1 Corinthians 15:51)

stops.hear: Tension builds in the choir
stops.happening: “zu der Zeit der letzten Posaune” (“at the last trump”)

stops.hear: Suddenly fast and loud, the whole orchestra in a storm
stops.happening: “Denn es wird die Posaune schallen” (“For the trumpet shall sound”), *Vivace*

stops.hear: The choir hurls out questions
stops.happening: “Tod, wo ist dein Stachel? Hölle, wo ist dein Sieg?” (“O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?”)

stops.hear: A broad, majestic fugue in C major
stops.happening: “Herr, du bist würdig” (“Thou art worthy, O Lord”, Revelation 4:11)

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: The fugue reaches its climax and ends in a blaze of C major
stops.happening: The triumphant end of the movement

notice: Count the voices entering at the start of the fugue: sopranos and altos, tenors, basses, each with the same broad tune.

movements.heading: Selig sind die Toten
movements.title: Selig sind die Toten
movements.summary: “Blessed are the dead which die in the Lord.” After the storm, calm. The sopranos begin high and slowly; the music grows warm and serene. At the end Brahms brings back the music of the first movement, and the harp returns: the last word of the work is the same as the first, “selig”, “blessed”.

mainIdeas.name: The opening
mainIdeas.description: the sopranos alone, a long, rising line, answered by the basses.

mainIdeas.name: The return
mainIdeas.description: the closing music of the first movement, with harp.

stops.hear: The sopranos sing a long, high, rising phrase; the basses answer
stops.happening: “Selig sind die Toten” (“Blessed are the dead”, Revelation 14:13)

stops.hear: A brighter key, a gentler movement
stops.happening: “Ja, der Geist spricht, dass sie ruhen von ihrer Arbeit” (“Yea, saith the Spirit, that they may rest from their labours”)

stops.hear: The opening words and melody return
stops.happening: “Selig sind die Toten” again

stops.hear: The harp returns, and the music of the first movement’s ending is heard again
stops.happening: The circle closes

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: Soft, rippling harp and a last, quiet “selig”
stops.happening: The same word that began the work ends it

notice: Compare the last minute with the last minute of the first movement. The music is almost the same; the words now speak of the dead instead of the mourners.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Otto Klemperer recorded the Requiem in Kingsway Hall in 1961 with two of the great German singers of the time, Elisabeth Schwarzkopf and Dietrich Fischer-Dieskau. Klemperer, then in his mid-seventies, takes slow, weighty tempi, which makes this one of the longer recordings.

threads.title: Comfort for the living
threads.body: Almost every movement moves from sorrow to consolation. Only the central fourth and the last are calm throughout.

threads.title: A symmetry
threads.body: The first and last movements begin “Selig sind” and share their ending; the second and sixth are the dramatic ones; the third and fifth begin with a soloist. The fourth stands in the middle.

threads.title: No dogma
threads.body: Brahms left out any mention of Christ’s death and redemption. When the cathedral’s music director in Bremen asked him to add it, he refused.
